Damian Paletta
 
What Darline Graham’s Runoff Win Means for November
 
Plus, Canada hits back at U.S. with new tariffs amid growing trade war, and CIA director makes surprise visit to Moscow
 
 
MEG KINNARD/AP
 

Good morning. The unexpectedly high-drama GOP Senate primary in South Carolina ended the way many projected it would six months ago: with a Graham as the nominee.

 

What perhaps no one foresaw is that the first name would be Darline. She will run for the seat held by her brother Lindsey for 23 years before he died in July.

 

Darline Graham’s victory over Rep. Ralph Norman in the runoff sets her up to take on the Democratic candidate, pediatrician Annie Andrews, in November. Andrews has never held elected office before.

 

Darline Graham is going to have to consolidate the GOP base to win in November. Her 52-48 margin in the GOP runoff suggests a very divided Republican electorate in South Carolina, with many people skeptical of her candidacy.

 

President Trump put a lot of political muscle into helping her win this nomination, and her victory shows that he still commands sway.

 

Lindsey Graham received 54% of the vote in the 2020 and 2014 elections, which wasn’t overwhelming but always led to comfortable victories over Democrats.

 

Darline Graham is going to have to prove herself to voters in the next two months, following her very rocky campaigning so far.

 

This isn’t a seat where Republicans want to be diverting a lot of money and staffing, as they will need to defend higher-pressure GOP seats in Texas, Maine, Iowa and elsewhere.

 

Darline Graham should be able to safely hold on to this seat. If it’s close in South Carolina, Republicans likely have much bigger problems across the country.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Doug Ford: The Ontario premier’s row with Trump is taking center stage in the trade conflict between the U.S. and Canada.

 

Trump’s Wednesday: The president is set for a live radio interview with Glenn Beck at 9 a.m. ET. He will hold a policy meeting at 3 p.m. and participate in a print interview at 4 p.m.

What I’m Following

 
 
VINCENT ALBAN/REUTERS
 

Canada hits back at the U.S. with fresh tariffs on American goods. Ottawa said it will impose tariffs of up to 50% on roughly 700 products worth about $20 billion as the acrimony between the U.S. and Canada grows over the collapse of trade talks. Among the products targeted by Canada are U.S. steel, aluminum, motorcycles, washers and dryers, chain saws, processed cheese, clams and frozen octopus.

 

CIA director pays a surprise Moscow visit. The agency declined to comment on John Ratcliffe’s first publicly known trip to the Russian capital, where he spent about four hours before leaving. The Tuesday visit came as the U.S. struggles to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran war.

 

Kevin Warsh wants to remake the Federal Reserve, but first he must explain the economy. The biggest call of his early Fed chairmanship is whether inflation can fall to 2% without higher rates. Warsh is going to Jackson Hole, Wyo., this week with an opportunity to explain whether rates are restrictive enough to keep inflation headed lower.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Trump submitted a landmark 30-year nuclear accord with Saudi Arabia to Congress for review.

 

• Trump threatened to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, in the latest escalation of tensions between the U.S. and Canada.

 

• New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration defended the launch of its new pied-à-terre tax in a legal filing.
